full_judgment:
Khondker Musa Khaled J: The petitioner Durga Rani Sutradhar of the original Miscellaneous Case No. 105 of 1986 (probate case) has preferred this appeal under section 299 of the Succession Act 1925 against the judgment and order dated 8-11-1989 passed by the learned District Judge. Narayanganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 13/88 affirming those of the learned Subordinate Judge passed on 6-4-1988 as District Delegate in the above mentioned original miscellaneous case. 

 2. The relevant facts giving rise to this appeal, in short, are that the petitioner Durga Rani Sutradhar wife of the deceased testator Hari Pada Sutradhar filed the above Will probate case before the District Delegate Subordinate Judge Narayanganj on 13-7-1986 under section 276 of the Succession Act 1925 (hereinafter will be referred to as Act) annexing the original Will and other supporting papers. On 6-8-1986 she had taken back the original Will replacing it by a photocopy with the permission of the court on condition of refilling the same. Unfortunately, the original Will was lost from her custody and she could not trace it out on search. 

 3. At the time of final hearing of the probate case the petitioner had to rely on a photostat copy of the 'Will' which was preserved by the petitioner and proved by her as well as attesting witness of the 'Will'. The OPs, sons of the testator, did not raise any objection to the grant of the probate in favour of their mother applicant. But the learned Subordinate Judge acting as a District Delegate, rejected the application on 6-8-1988 after ex parte hearing only on the ground that the intended probate cannot be granted without having the original 'Will' submitted and proved. Thereafter, the petitioner preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 13/88 which was also dismissed more or less on the same ground of the non-availability of the original 'Will' with the finding that probate cannot be granted on the basis of photostat copy of the 'Will' and accordingly affirmed the judgment and order passed by the District Delegate. 

 4. As such, the applicant of the probate case has preferred this appeal mainly on the ground that the learned courts below committed an error of law in holding that without having the original 'Will', no probate can be granted. It has not been considered by the courts below that the original 'Will' was once submitted in the court and when it was found missing, the petitioner relied on photo copy and adduced evidence to prove genuineness of the same and none denied as to the genuineness of the "Will' in question. 

 10. We have carefully gone through the sections 237, 238 and 239 available in Chapter II of the Act. The section 237 provides that when a 'Will' is lost, mislaid or destroyed by accident and destroyed by the act of testator himself and a copy or even a draft is available, probate may be granted of such copy or draft for limited duration until the original or authenticated copy is produced. In such cases, the copy of the lost "Will' may be admitted as a secondary evidence under section 65 of the Evidence Act. 

 11. The following section 238 deals with cases where no copy of the lost 'Will' has been preserved. In that case also probate may be granted of the contents of the lost "Will' if genuine execution of the lost 'Will' can be established properly by evidence. 

 13. Now, turning to the relevant provision for submitting an application for the grant of probate, it appears that the exceptions to the general procedure of filing original 'Will' along with the application are available with reference to the cases falling under sections 237, 238 and 239 of the Act. The section 276 of the Act runs as follows: 

 Section 276 "Petition for probate-(1) Application for probate or for letters of administration, with the will annexed, shall be made by a petition distinctly written in English or in the language in ordinary use in proceedings before the Court in which the application is made, with the will or, in the cases mentioned in sections 237, 238 and 239, a copy, draft, or statement of the contents thereof annexed, and stating- 

 14. So, it is evident from the above legal provisions that the original 'Will' need not be annexed with the application for probate in respect of eases mentioned in section 237, 238 and 239 or" the Act. In such cases of non-availability of the original 'Will' a draft copy or statement of the contents thereof may be annexed. Under those circumstances, production of original 'Will' is not indispensable Therefore; it appears that an application for grant of probate is legally permissible even without existence of the original 'Will' before the court. The learned court below appears to have overlooked this specific legal provision as contemplated under section 237 of the Act, which is very much applicable in this case. If the conditions attached to the grant of probate are not fulfilled, it may be rejected, but the case is required to be considered on the basis of photo copy when the original is proved to have been lost. 

 15. In the instance of the case, the petitioner appears to have filed original 'Will' when the case was initiated on 30-7-1986. The order No.2 of the original case record shows that on 6-8-1986 she was permitted by the court to receive back the original 'Will' by filing a photostat copy. The record shows that the learned Advocate had taken back the original 'Will' by putting signature on the firisti". Thereafter, the original 'Will' was lost from the custody of the petitioner and a photocopy of the 'Will' is available with the record, which bears the seal of the Subordinate Judge Court, Narayanganj with date of filing as on 30-7-1986. So, the photocopy of original 'Will' cannot be thrown away outright as the courts below did in the present case. In view of the section 337 of the Act, the courts ought to have considered the photocopy and arrived at the findings as to the genuineness of the execution of the lost 'Will' how and when it was lost, whether such loss of 'Will' was after the death of the testator, and correctness of contents available in the copy of the 'Will' on the basis of evidence on record. But none of these essential aspects has been adjudicated by the learned courts below. It may be noted here that secondary evidence of the existence, condition and contents of the original is admissible under section 65 of the Evidence Act when the original 'Will' has been destroyed or lost. The burden of proving due execution is on the propounder assessable on the preponderance of evidence. In such view of the matter, the decision of the courts below cannot be legally sustained. 

 17. Before parting with the case, we consider it necessary to discuss some relevant provisions of the Act for having a clear conception as to the procedure of dealing with a probate case. The learned District Judge appears to have entertained appeal from the order of the learned District Delegate without having any such scope in the legal provisions of the Act. There is no provision in the Act empowering the District Judge to hear appeal from the order passed by the District Delegate. Vesting of such power is not necessary too. The District Delegate has no authority to pass any order refusing grant of probate. Section 272 of the Act provides that the District Delegate is only authorised to grant probate where there is no contentions or challenge against probate of the 'Will'. Section 286 of the Act imposes restriction on the power of the District Delegate allowing only dealing with a non-contentious proceeding. Even in the non-contentious case, if, in the opinion of the District Delegate, there is doubt as to whether probate should be granted he shall return the application for presentation to the District Judge or he shall send it to the District Judge directly under section 288. Any proceeding taken in the District Delegate’s Court on contest is without jurisdiction. In such contentious case, the District, Judge shall deal with the matter under section 295 of the Act, treating the same as a regular suit. 

 Section 288. "Procedure where there is contention or District Delegate thinks probate or letters of administration should be refused in his Court. In every case in which there is contention, or the District Delegate is of opinion that the probate or letters of administration should be refused in his Court, the petition, with any documents which may have been filed therewith, shall be returned to the person by whom the application was made, in order that the same may be presented to the District Judge, unless the District Delegate thinks it necessary, for the purposes of justice, to impound the same, which he is hereby authorised to do; and, in that case, the same shall be sent by him to the District Judge" 

 19. Thus it appears that the District Delegate is not a in position to reject the application for probate irrespective of the fact whether it is contested one or not So, the question of preferring appeal from the order of the District Delegate to the District Judge can hardly arise. No. such provision has been prescribed in the Act too. Only the order passed by the District Judge is made appealable to the High Court Division under section 299 of the Act. So, it appears that not only the court of District Delegate committed mistake in rejecting the probate case without legal authority to do so, but the District Judge also illegally entertained the appeal from the order of the District Delegate without adhering to the provision of law. 

 20. Be that as it may, it is evident that the OPs of the probate case did not appear and none had raised any objection to the grant of probate in question. So, it was not a contentious matter and the District Delegate is quite competent to deal with the case. If he finds any doubt which may lead to the rejection of the probate case, he would follow the procedure laid down in section 288 of the Act already discussed above. 

 21. For the reasons stated above, the judgments and orders of both the courts below are liable to be set aside. Since the probate case has not been disposed of on merit and further evidence may be necessary there is no way out but to send the case back on remand for proper adjudication of the necessary points in issue, which have already been pointed out previously. However, the trial Court will be at liberty to issue fresh citation summons on the OPs if it is felt necessary and also allow the petitioner to adduce more evidence to prove her case, if the case does not become contentious, or doubtful, and dispose of the case in accordance with law. 

 In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgments and orders passed by the courts below are set aside. The case is sent back on remand to the learned District Delegate. Subordinate Judge through the District Judge, Narayanganj for holding fresh trial in accordance with law and in the light of our observations given above. We prefer to make no order as to cost.
